1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.
18

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

<!-- Field of the Disclosure - body text only, no heading line. -->

The present disclosure relates to power tools for installing tiles, slabs, panels and other covering elements, whether guided by hand or drawn across the work by a flexible pulling element, and more particularly to a vibration device that transmits mechanical vibration into a covering element that has been placed on a bed of thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material, in order to release trapped air, distribute the bonding material and seat the covering element against its substrate.

content.content:
1	<!-- Background - body text only, no heading line. -->
2	
3	When a tile, slab or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
4	
5	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place.
6	
7	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
8	
9	An example of the vibrating suction-cup approach applied to tiling is described in [REF:DE-202021002652-U1], which discloses a device provided with a handle for lifting and laying slabs, in particular tiles, having two shafts slidably connected in the handle, at least one electrically operated pump for generating a negative pressure in suction cups at the free ends of the shafts, and at least one electric motor for generating vibration of the shafts, the suction cup being formed by a rubber-elastic apron. The negative pressure in that device is developed inside a rubber-elastic cup. A head shell is connected at the free end of each vibrated shaft and carries that cup on its underside, so that the member presented to the tile is a compliant cup.
10	
11	Attaching a body to a surface by reducing the pressure in a space bounded by a compliant peripheral wall is also known outside the tiling field. [REF:US-11408462-B2] describes an adhesion device that defines a decompression space between a wall surface and the device, in which the peripheral wall of the decompression space is formed by elastic partitions, the wall-surface-side end of the partition nearest the wall surface contacting the wall surface, together with a restricting member of higher rigidity placed on that partition to restrict it from being deformed into the decompression space as the space becomes negatively pressured. The rigidity there is added to keep a compliant partition in shape; the member that meets the wall surface remains an elastic one. [REF:US-4934475-A] describes a device for moving along a wall surface having a main body, a seal member, a pressure reduction space defined by the seal in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means for discharging fluid from that space, and vibration generating means; there, the vibration generating means imparts a lifting force to the main body in a direction away from the wall surface so as to reduce the suction-adhering force, and imparts a moving force that moves the body along the wall.
12	
13	Vacuum handling equipment for sheet goods holds the workpiece through a suction surface applied flat against it. [REF:US-11247858-B2] describes a vacuum plate lifting system having a substantially horizontal suction plate with a perforated suction lifting surface, an airflow suction system for conveying vacuum air pressure to that surface, and an elongate bar carrying nozzles that is movable between a raised orientation and a lowered orientation so that a suction airflow sweeps dust or debris from the surface beneath. [REF:US-10001245-B2] describes a base assembly having a cup-shaped portion that defines a cavity on its second side and a pneumatic generator in flow communication with the cavity, the pneumatic generator being operable in a suction mode and a blower mode: in the suction mode the second side is securely coupleable to the surface by vacuum force, and in the blower mode the second side is movable substantially frictionlessly across the surface on an air cushion. Holding and moving are alternative states of that apparatus, which holds when it is not sliding and slides when it is not holding, and a control is provided to switch between them.
14	
15	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
16	
17	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
18

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. [REF:US-11408462-B2] describes an adhesion device that defines a decompression space between a wall surface and the device, in which the peripheral wall of the decompression space is formed by elastic partitions, the wall-surface-side end of the partition nearest the wall surface contacting the wall surface, together with a restricting member of higher rigidity placed on that partition to restrict it from being deformed into the decompression space as the space becomes negatively pressured. 1	<!-- Summary - body text only, no heading line. -->
2	
3	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.
4	
5	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The rate it delivers at the intended working pressure difference is at least equal to the rate at which ambient air passes through the clearance at that same pressure difference, so the chamber falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two flow rates balance, and it stays there for as long as the mechanism runs even though air never stops entering. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.
6	
7	Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base, while the operator's hands carry less.
8	
9	Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.
10	
11	In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small in-plane pulling force applied by the operator, while the force normal to the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.
12	
13	A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
14

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The rate it delivers at the intended working pressure difference is at least equal to the rate at which ambient air passes through the clearance at that same pressure difference, so the chamber falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two flow rates balance, and it stays there for as long as the mechanism runs even though air never stops entering. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small in-plane pulling force applied by the operator, while the force normal to the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

1	<!-- Detailed Description - body text only, no heading line. -->
2	
3	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
4	
5	Overview
6	
7	FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use. A covering element 36, which may be a ceramic or porcelain tile, a stone slab, a large-format panel or a similar rigid covering element, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 may be a floor screed, a wall, a backer board or any other surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and seats the covering element 36 to the intended height.
8	
9	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
10	
11	The base
12	
13	The base 12 is a rigid plate. It is rigid in the sense that matters here: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished. Suitable materials are metals such as aluminium alloy or steel, and rigid engineering plastics. The base 12 is shown as a flat plate of constant thickness; it may equally be ribbed, dished or box-sectioned on the first side 14 to raise its stiffness without adding mass.
14	
15	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.
16	
17	The vibration motor
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. The fasteners 54 are shown in FIG. 1. That direct mounting is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
20	
21	The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12, including an electric motor driving an eccentric mass, a pneumatic vibrator, and a linear oscillator. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the vibration motor 18 is a housing standing directly on the base 12, wider along the long edge of the base 12 than it is tall. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the duct 32 and the extraction opening 30, discharging it to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet on the pump housing. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 is self-contained and no hose runs back to a separate machine. The duct 32 is an upright hollow column open at both ends that stands on the first side 14 over the extraction opening 30 and carries the air-extraction mechanism 20 on its upper end, so that the column is interposed between the pump and the base 12 and the whole of the withdrawn air passes up through it from the chamber 22 into the pump. Other air-extraction mechanisms 20 that withdraw air from the chamber 22 may be used, including a fan or blower, or an ejector supplied with compressed air.
26	
27	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is devoid of a valve operable to close the chamber 22 to atmosphere, and there is nothing in which a vacuum could be held. As explained below, the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
28	
29	An electrical supply 50 provides power to the vibration motor 18 and, where the air-extraction mechanism 20 is electrically driven, to the air-extraction mechanism 20. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the electrical supply 50 is a flexible cord leaving the air-extraction mechanism 20 and running to a mains or site supply; a battery carried on the base 12 may be used instead. The vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 may be switched together or independently of one another.
30	
31	The perimeter member and the chamber
32	
33	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a continuous closed loop, unbroken at the corners, standing a little inboard of the outer edge of the base 12 so that a plain margin of the second side 16 lies outside the loop, as seen in the bottom plan view. The loop may equally run at the very edge of the base 12, its outer side coinciding with that edge and leaving no such margin. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly fixed to the base 12 by fasteners, or is formed integrally with the base 12 as one piece; either way the joint between them is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss.
34	
35	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. In the embodiment of FIG. 4, the perimeter member 24 is a metal loop carrying a low-friction facing 28 of PTFE bonded or mechanically fixed to its end, and the exposed surface of the low-friction facing 28 forms the bearing face 26; the low-friction facing 28 is thin and hard, and being a rigid plastic rather than an elastomer it does not act as a spring in the vibration path. In another embodiment the perimeter member 24 is made in one piece of a low-friction rigid plastic, and the bearing face 26 is simply the end face of that member. The bearing face 26 lies in a single plane, so that the vibration device 10 sits flat on a planar exposed face 38 and the load is shared around the whole loop.
36	
37	The low-friction facing 28 may be flush with the outer and inner sides of the perimeter member 24, or it may stand a little proud of one or both of them; where it stands proud, the bearing face 26 is correspondingly wider than the loop that carries it. The width of the bearing face 26, measured from its outer side to its inner side, governs two things at once, and is chosen with both in view: it sets the contact pressure at which the holding force is delivered into the exposed face 38, and, because the clearance 34 described below runs beneath that width, it sets the length of the flow path through which ambient air must pass to reach the chamber 22 and hence the flow resistance of that path. A wider bearing face 26 spreads the contact and lengthens the leakage path; a narrower one concentrates the contact and shortens it.
38	
39	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
40	
41	Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.
42	
43	The flow balance that holds the device down
44	
45	The pressure in the chamber 22 is set by a balance of two flows. Ambient air enters the chamber 22 through the clearance 34 at an inflow rate that depends on the flow resistance of the clearance 34 and on how far the chamber 22 is below atmospheric pressure. The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the extraction opening 30 at a volumetric extraction rate. Both quantities vary with the pressure in the chamber 22, and they vary in opposite directions: as the chamber 22 is drawn down, the inflow through the clearance 34 rises, because the pressure difference driving it rises, while the volumetric extraction rate falls, because the air-extraction mechanism 20 is working against a greater pressure difference. The chamber 22 therefore falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two rates have become equal. That steady state is maintained for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs, notwithstanding that ambient air is entering the chamber 22 the whole time.
46	
47	The pressure at which the chamber 22 settles is the working pressure difference, and it is what the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sized to reach. The vibration device 10 is designed for a working pressure difference that produces a holding force adequate to hold it against the covering element 36, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 is then chosen so that the rate it delivers at that working pressure difference is at least equal to the rate at which ambient air passes through the clearance 34 at the same pressure difference. Both rates are taken at the same pressure difference, so the comparison is between like and like, and meeting it places the crossing point of the two curves at or beyond the intended working pressure difference, which is what draws the chamber 22 down at least that far.
48	
49	The rate an air-extraction mechanism 20 delivers against a pressure difference is not always to hand, whereas its free-air displacement, the volumetric rate it delivers with no pressure difference across it, is a figure commonly quoted for pumps, fans and blowers. Free-air displacement may therefore be used to make a first selection, provided a margin is allowed for the fall in delivered rate with rising pressure difference, and the choice is then confirmed against the delivered rate at the working pressure difference.
50	
51	The condition that matters in use is therefore expressed as follows throughout this description: the volumetric extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34. The delivered-rate rule set out above is one way of meeting that condition, and it is the way used in the embodiments described here. The two statements describe different stages: the rule is applied when the air-extraction mechanism 20 is selected, comparing the rate it delivers at the intended working pressure difference against the flow the clearance 34 passes at that same pressure difference, while the condition that matters in use is met throughout operation, at a steady state in which the two rates have become equal and it is the pressure difference that has become steady.
52	
53	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.
54	
55	Two properties of this arrangement should be noted, because they are what the arrangement is for.
56	
57	First, the holding force is self-restoring rather than fragile. In an apparatus that relies on a sealed enclosure, any breach of the seal, such as a chip in the exposed face 38, a grain of bonding material 40 caught under the perimeter, or a moment of tilting as the device passes a lippage step between two covering elements 36, releases the vacuum and drops the device. Here the enclosure is already open, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is already running against a continuous inflow, and an increase in the size of the clearance 34 simply moves the steady state to a slightly higher chamber pressure and a slightly lower holding force. The vibration device 10 does not have to be re-attached; it does not have a state of being attached at all, only a state of being held.
58	
59	Second, and for the same reason, the vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and slides under the holding force with a modest in-plane resistance, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No mode has to be switched, no air cushion has to be raised under the device, and no grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36 at full amplitude, instead of falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
60	
61	The vibration transmission path
62	
63	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 through the direct fixing at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the low-friction facing 28 forming the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
64	
65	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area and from one operator to the next.
66	
67	The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film, being compressible, both stores and dissipates part of what crosses it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
68	
69	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
70	
71	Handles
72	
73	One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and to lift and carry the vibration device 10 between covering elements 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
74	
75	In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the handle 44 is a single bail standing on the base 12 clear of the vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20. Two side grips, one at each side of the base 12, may be used instead.
76	
77	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
78	
79	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10 at an attachment formation 48 on the base 12. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
80	
81	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. Because the attachment formation 48 is placed low, as described below, the line along which the tension acts lies close to the plane of the exposed face 38. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and is arranged to apply to the vibration device 10 a pulling force substantially in the plane of the exposed face 38. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls. The operator may stand away from the vibration device 10, and at a large working distance need not bend over it at all.
82	
83	In the embodiment of FIG. 5 the attachment formation 48 is placed low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26, so that the line of the applied tension lies near that plane and produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24. More than one attachment formation 48 may be provided, for instance one at each end of the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 can be drawn in either direction without being turned about.
84	
85	Further variations
86	
87	A particulate separator may be fitted in the duct 32 between the extraction opening 30 and the air-extraction mechanism 20, to keep dust and grains of bonding material 40 drawn in through the clearance 34 out of the air-extraction mechanism 20.
88	
89	The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. It may instead be divided into two or more chambers 22 by rigid walls standing on the second side 16, each of the chambers 22 being in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20. Dividing the chamber 22 in this way keeps the pressure differential more uniform beneath a base 12 of large plan area, because each of the chambers 22 is fed by its own extraction opening 30 and the pressure in it does not depend on flow travelling the whole width of the base 12. Rigid walls used in this way also stiffen the base 12 against the alternating force from the vibration motor 18, and, standing on the second side 16 with their lower ends in the plane of the bearing face 26, they add further rigid contact area through which vibration passes into the covering element 36.
90	
91	The perimeter member 24 is shown as a rectangular loop in FIG. 3. It may equally be circular, oval or any other closed shape.
92	
93	The vibration device 10 has been described in use on a horizontal floor, where the holding force acts downward and only the in-plane resistance of the bearing face 26 has to be overcome to move it. It may also be used on a wall or other inclined or vertical surface. There the frictional resistance developed at the bearing face 26 by the holding force must additionally support the weight of the vibration device 10, and the choice of the material of the bearing face 26 becomes a compromise: the lower its coefficient of friction, the more easily the vibration device 10 is drawn across the exposed face 38, and the greater the holding force needed to keep it from sliding down under its own weight. For use on vertical surfaces the holding force is therefore raised, by increasing the plan area of the chamber 22 or the extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20, rather than by giving up the low-friction bearing face 26 on which the sliding depends.
94	
95	Method of use
96	
97	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. Before the vibration device 10 is placed on the covering element 36, the method begins with spreading bonding material 40 on a substrate 42 and laying a covering element 36 on the spread bonding material 40. It continues with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44. The method ends with stopping the air-extraction mechanism 20, whereupon the pressure in the chamber 22 returns to atmospheric through the clearance 34, the holding force falls away, and the vibration device 10 lifts off the exposed face 38 freely. The vibration device 10 is worked over the covering element 36 until the covering element 36 has settled to the intended height and the bonding material 40 has been distributed beneath it; it is then moved to the next covering element 36 and the sequence is repeated.
98
