In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use. A covering element 36, which may be a ceramic or porcelain tile, a stone slab, a large-format panel or a similar rigid covering element, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 may be a floor screed, a wall, a backer board or any other surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and seats the covering element 36 to the intended height.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is a rigid plate. It is rigid in the sense that matters here: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished. Suitable materials are metals such as aluminium alloy or steel, and rigid engineering plastics. The base 12 is shown as a flat plate of constant thickness; it may equally be ribbed, dished or box-sectioned on the first side 14 to raise its stiffness without adding mass.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. The fasteners 54 are shown in FIG. 1. That direct mounting is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12, including an electric motor driving an eccentric mass, a pneumatic vibrator, and a linear oscillator. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the vibration motor 18 is a housing standing directly on the base 12, wider along the long edge of the base 12 than it is tall. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the duct 32 and the extraction opening 30, discharging it to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet on the pump housing. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 is self-contained and no hose runs back to a separate machine. The duct 32 is an upright hollow column open at both ends that stands on the first side 14 over the extraction opening 30 and carries the air-extraction mechanism 20 on its upper end, so that the column is interposed between the pump and the base 12 and the whole of the withdrawn air passes up through it from the chamber 22 into the pump. Other air-extraction mechanisms 20 that withdraw air from the chamber 22 may be used, including a fan or blower, or an ejector supplied with compressed air.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is devoid of a valve operable to close the chamber 22 to atmosphere, and there is nothing in which a vacuum could be held. As explained below, the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

An electrical supply 50 provides power to the vibration motor 18 and, where the air-extraction mechanism 20 is electrically driven, to the air-extraction mechanism 20. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the electrical supply 50 is a flexible cord leaving the air-extraction mechanism 20 and running to a mains or site supply; a battery carried on the base 12 may be used instead. The vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 may be switched together or independently of one another.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a continuous closed loop, unbroken at the corners, standing a little inboard of the outer edge of the base 12 so that a plain margin of the second side 16 lies outside the loop, as seen in the bottom plan view. The loop may equally run at the very edge of the base 12, its outer side coinciding with that edge and leaving no such margin. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly fixed to the base 12 by fasteners, or is formed integrally with the base 12 as one piece; either way the joint between them is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. In the embodiment of FIG. 4, the perimeter member 24 is a metal loop carrying a low-friction facing 28 of PTFE bonded or mechanically fixed to its end, and the exposed surface of the low-friction facing 28 forms the bearing face 26; the low-friction facing 28 is thin and hard, and being a rigid plastic rather than an elastomer it does not act as a spring in the vibration path. In another embodiment the perimeter member 24 is made in one piece of a low-friction rigid plastic, and the bearing face 26 is simply the end face of that member. The bearing face 26 lies in a single plane, so that the vibration device 10 sits flat on a planar exposed face 38 and the load is shared around the whole loop.

The low-friction facing 28 may be flush with the outer and inner sides of the perimeter member 24, or it may stand a little proud of one or both of them; where it stands proud, the bearing face 26 is correspondingly wider than the loop that carries it. The width of the bearing face 26, measured from its outer side to its inner side, governs two things at once, and is chosen with both in view: it sets the contact pressure at which the holding force is delivered into the exposed face 38, and, because the clearance 34 described below runs beneath that width, it sets the length of the flow path through which ambient air must pass to reach the chamber 22 and hence the flow resistance of that path. A wider bearing face 26 spreads the contact and lengthens the leakage path; a narrower one concentrates the contact and shortens it.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.

The flow balance that holds the device down

The pressure in the chamber 22 is set by a balance of two flows. Ambient air enters the chamber 22 through the clearance 34 at an inflow rate that depends on the flow resistance of the clearance 34 and on how far the chamber 22 is below atmospheric pressure. The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the extraction opening 30 at a volumetric extraction rate. Both quantities vary with the pressure in the chamber 22, and they vary in opposite directions: as the chamber 22 is drawn down, the inflow through the clearance 34 rises, because the pressure difference driving it rises, while the volumetric extraction rate falls, because the air-extraction mechanism 20 is working against a greater pressure difference. The chamber 22 therefore falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two rates have become equal. That steady state is maintained for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs, notwithstanding that ambient air is entering the chamber 22 the whole time.

The pressure at which the chamber 22 settles is the working pressure difference, and it is what the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sized to reach. The vibration device 10 is designed for a working pressure difference that produces a holding force adequate to hold it against the covering element 36, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 is then chosen so that the rate it delivers at that working pressure difference is at least equal to the rate at which ambient air passes through the clearance 34 at the same pressure difference. Both rates are taken at the same pressure difference, so the comparison is between like and like, and meeting it places the crossing point of the two curves at or beyond the intended working pressure difference, which is what draws the chamber 22 down at least that far.

The rate an air-extraction mechanism 20 delivers against a pressure difference is not always to hand, whereas its free-air displacement, the volumetric rate it delivers with no pressure difference across it, is a figure commonly quoted for pumps, fans and blowers. Free-air displacement may therefore be used to make a first selection, provided a margin is allowed for the fall in delivered rate with rising pressure difference, and the choice is then confirmed against the delivered rate at the working pressure difference.

The condition that matters in use is therefore expressed as follows throughout this description: the volumetric extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34. The delivered-rate rule set out above is one way of meeting that condition, and it is the way used in the embodiments described here. The two statements describe different stages: the rule is applied when the air-extraction mechanism 20 is selected, comparing the rate it delivers at the intended working pressure difference against the flow the clearance 34 passes at that same pressure difference, while the condition that matters in use is met throughout operation, at a steady state in which the two rates have become equal and it is the pressure difference that has become steady.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

Two properties of this arrangement should be noted, because they are what the arrangement is for.

First, the holding force is self-restoring rather than fragile. In an apparatus that relies on a sealed enclosure, any breach of the seal, such as a chip in the exposed face 38, a grain of bonding material 40 caught under the perimeter, or a moment of tilting as the device passes a lippage step between two covering elements 36, releases the vacuum and drops the device. Here the enclosure is already open, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is already running against a continuous inflow, and an increase in the size of the clearance 34 simply moves the steady state to a slightly higher chamber pressure and a slightly lower holding force. The vibration device 10 does not have to be re-attached; it does not have a state of being attached at all, only a state of being held.

Second, and for the same reason, the vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and slides under the holding force with a modest in-plane resistance, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No mode has to be switched, no air cushion has to be raised under the device, and no grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36 at full amplitude, instead of falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 through the direct fixing at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the low-friction facing 28 forming the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area and from one operator to the next.

The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film, being compressible, both stores and dissipates part of what crosses it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and to lift and carry the vibration device 10 between covering elements 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the handle 44 is a single bail standing on the base 12 clear of the vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20. Two side grips, one at each side of the base 12, may be used instead.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10 at an attachment formation 48 on the base 12. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. Because the attachment formation 48 is placed low, as described below, the line along which the tension acts lies close to the plane of the exposed face 38. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and is arranged to apply to the vibration device 10 a pulling force substantially in the plane of the exposed face 38. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls. The operator may stand away from the vibration device 10, and at a large working distance need not bend over it at all.

In the embodiment of FIG. 5 the attachment formation 48 is placed low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26, so that the line of the applied tension lies near that plane and produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24. More than one attachment formation 48 may be provided, for instance one at each end of the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 can be drawn in either direction without being turned about.

Further variations

A particulate separator may be fitted in the duct 32 between the extraction opening 30 and the air-extraction mechanism 20, to keep dust and grains of bonding material 40 drawn in through the clearance 34 out of the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. It may instead be divided into two or more chambers 22 by rigid walls standing on the second side 16, each of the chambers 22 being in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20. Dividing the chamber 22 in this way keeps the pressure differential more uniform beneath a base 12 of large plan area, because each of the chambers 22 is fed by its own extraction opening 30 and the pressure in it does not depend on flow travelling the whole width of the base 12. Rigid walls used in this way also stiffen the base 12 against the alternating force from the vibration motor 18, and, standing on the second side 16 with their lower ends in the plane of the bearing face 26, they add further rigid contact area through which vibration passes into the covering element 36.

The perimeter member 24 is shown as a rectangular loop in FIG. 3. It may equally be circular, oval or any other closed shape.

The vibration device 10 has been described in use on a horizontal floor, where the holding force acts downward and only the in-plane resistance of the bearing face 26 has to be overcome to move it. It may also be used on a wall or other inclined or vertical surface. There the frictional resistance developed at the bearing face 26 by the holding force must additionally support the weight of the vibration device 10, and the choice of the material of the bearing face 26 becomes a compromise: the lower its coefficient of friction, the more easily the vibration device 10 is drawn across the exposed face 38, and the greater the holding force needed to keep it from sliding down under its own weight. For use on vertical surfaces the holding force is therefore raised, by increasing the plan area of the chamber 22 or the extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20, rather than by giving up the low-friction bearing face 26 on which the sliding depends.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. Before the vibration device 10 is placed on the covering element 36, the method begins with spreading bonding material 40 on a substrate 42 and laying a covering element 36 on the spread bonding material 40. It continues with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44. The method ends with stopping the air-extraction mechanism 20, whereupon the pressure in the chamber 22 returns to atmospheric through the clearance 34, the holding force falls away, and the vibration device 10 lifts off the exposed face 38 freely. The vibration device 10 is worked over the covering element 36 until the covering element 36 has settled to the intended height and the bonding material 40 has been distributed beneath it; it is then moved to the next covering element 36 and the sequence is repeated.

translating the vibration device across the exposed face, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face over the exposed face, so that the vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element.

21. The method of claim 20, wherein the pressure differential is maintained continuously while the vibration device is translated across the exposed face, so that the vibration device is held against the covering element and slid over the exposed face at the same time.

22. The method of claim 20, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by applying tension to a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device.

23. The method of claim 20, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle coupled to the first side, and wherein no downward force is applied to the vibration device by an operator while the vibration motor operates.

24. The method of claim 20, further comprising stopping the air-extraction mechanism after the vibration device has been translated across the exposed face, whereupon pressure in the chamber returns to atmospheric pressure through the clearance and the vibration device is released from the exposed face.

25. The method of claim 20, further comprising spreading the bonding material on a substrate and laying the covering element on the spread bonding material before the vibration device is placed on the exposed face.

26. The method of claim 20, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is polytetrafluoroethylene.

The draft was already substantially complete; the prior failure was an interrupted run, not a content defect. I verified the whole package and made two consistency repairs.

**Verification performed**

- Numerals: all 22 table entries (10 through 54) are used in the specification, each against one part name; the union of the five figure sheets covers exactly those 22, with no numeral on a sheet that is missing from the table. Sheet loads are 8, 8, 3, 8, 4, all within the eight-numeral limit.
- Figure/text synchronization: FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 are each recited in the Brief Description and in the Detailed Description, and each part described as visible in a figure is listed on that figure's sheet.
- Filing cleanliness: no drafting note, placeholder, bracketed request, question, human-directed instruction, or em dash anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`. Cross-Reference reads `Not applicable.` Citations appear only in the Background and use only the five INDEX keys.
- Prior-art fidelity: I re-read all five references and confirmed each Background characterization against the file text, including the nozzle bar and the dust/debris sweeping method in [REF:US-11247858-B2], which appear in that file's claims rather than its abstract.

**Changes made**

1. `draft/07-detailed-description.md`: the single-extraction-opening sentence attributed extraction opening 30 to FIG. 1, whose sheet does not carry that numeral. It now reads "In the embodiment shown there is a single extraction opening 30 ... seen in FIG. 2 and FIG. 3, with the duct 32 ... and the vibration motor 18 ... both seen in FIG. 1", which matches the sheet assignments exactly.
2. `draft/07-detailed-description.md`: "fixed to the base 12 by fasteners" now reads "by fasteners 54", so the part is not named a second time without its numeral.

I left the claims, numeral definitions, disclosed embodiments, and figure plan untouched, since nothing in the review or in my checks required a change to them.

input.summary: Resumed the saved candidate and ran the full consistency pass over text, claims, numerals, figures, and citations. The application was already complete: nine sections, 26 claims in three statutory classes, a 22-entry numeral table, and five figure briefs. I made two internal-consistency repairs in the Detailed Description: extraction opening 30 was attributed to FIG. 1, whose sheet does not carry that numeral, so the sentence now points 30 to FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 and points duct 32 and vibration motor 18 to FIG. 1; and the second mention of the fasteners now carries numeral 54 rather than naming the part without it. Everything else was left alone. The one item in the review, a drafting run that produced no result with exit code 143, was an interrupted process rather than a defect in the text, so there was nothing in the files to repair for it beyond finishing the verification the interrupted run never reached.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries the invention on a rigid, deliberately non-sealing perimeter member whose low-friction bearing face contacts the tile while a clearance remains along at least part of it, combined with an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air keeps flowing in through that clearance. Every reference in prior_art/ that reduces pressure under a body does it by closing the space: DE-202021002652-U1 uses a rubber-elastic apron suction cup, US-11408462-B2 puts an elastic partition against the wall and only stiffens it with a rigidity member above, US-4934475-A recites a seal member defining the pressure reduction space, and US-11247858-B2 pulls vacuum through a perforated suction plate laid flat on the sheet. A perimeter that is admitted to leak, and a pump sized against that leak, is what none of them has.

The all-rigid vibration transmission path limitation in claim 1 is what clears DE-202021002652-U1 specifically, since that document vibrates shafts that terminate in head shells carrying rubber-elastic suction cups, so a compliant member sits in its own transmission path. The negative recitation, no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, is stated in the same words in the Detailed Description under 'The vibration transmission path'.

The slidable-while-held limitation clears US-10001245-B2, whose pneumatic generator holds in suction mode and floats the plate on an air cushion in blower mode with a control to switch between them. Holding and sliding there are alternative states. The specification says in terms that holding and sliding are simultaneous here and that no mode has to be switched, which is the sentence a later argument would be built from. It also clears US-4934475-A, where the vibration is used to lift the body and reduce the suction-adhering force so the device walks along the wall; here the vibration is the payload delivered into the tile and the hold is never reduced.

Left out of claim 1 deliberately: the handle, the flexible pulling element, the attachment formation, the duct and extraction opening, the vacuum-pump species, PTFE, the valveless chamber, and the delivered-rate sizing rule. None of them is needed to distinguish the art or to make the invention work, and each is available as a dependent fallback (claims 3, 4, 7, 9, 10, 13, 14).

The independent system claim 15 is where the decoupled-control embodiment lives, because a rope-drawn device is sold and used by different parties than a hand-guided one. It recites that the flexible pulling element is incapable of transmitting compression and applies force substantially in the plane of the exposed face, which is the structural reason the operator cannot be pressing the tool down. Method claim 20 covers the installer's acts.

The two edits this turn were both figure-to-text alignment, not substance. Attributing extraction opening 30 to FIG. 1 was wrong on the face of the figure plan, since FIG. 1 is a perspective from above and the opening is on the underside; FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 are the sheets that carry it. Naming the fasteners a second time without numeral 54 left a part named in the text whose numeral exists in the table, which is the exact condition the numeral check looks for.

I did not add dependent claims for the divided chambers, the multiple extraction openings, or the vertical-surface use, although the description supports all three. The standing instruction across this candidate has been to preserve claim substance, and the request this turn was to finish the checks rather than to widen the ladder. Those three are available if the attorney wants them later.

input.prior_art_strategy: All five references were read in full before drafting and re-read this turn to confirm every Background statement against the file text, including the nozzle-carrying bar and the sweep-dust-or-debris method of US-11247858-B2, which appear in that file's claims rather than its abstract. The Background walks through the art in the order of the problem it leaves unsolved: the vibrating rubber-elastic suction cup of DE-202021002652-U1, the elastic partitions with a rigidity-restricting member of US-11408462-B2, the seal member plus vibration-driven walking of US-4934475-A, and the two vacuum handling systems, US-11247858-B2 with its perforated suction plate and US-10001245-B2 with its mutually exclusive suction and blower modes. Every one of them closes the enclosed space with a compliant member or a flat perforated plate, and none has a reason to open it. The independent claims therefore turn on the opposite choice: a rigid low-friction perimeter that restricts inflow without stopping it, an extraction mechanism sized against that continuous inflow, an all-rigid path from motor to tile, and holding and sliding occurring at the same time rather than as switched modes. The specification states the technical problem each of those solves, the self-restoring hold across lippage steps and grains of bonding material, the removal of the operator from the load path rather than damping, and the leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it, so the arguments exist in the description before they are needed. Terminology was chosen away from the art's vocabulary: perimeter member and bearing face rather than seal, skirt, cup or partition; chamber rather than decompression space or pressure reduction space; air-extraction mechanism rather than pneumatic generator or vacuum creating means.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole assembly standing on that tile, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing toward its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. Identified within that front side face, in the half of the face nearer the right end of the slab and midway up the height of the face, so the point lies at the end of the slab remote from the ring, and not on the ring, the cord, either housing, the column, the floor or a joint line.

**View:** Greatly enlarged fragmentary vertical section through the lower end of a perimeter member of the kind shown in FIG. 2, at a place where the clearance is present, with the bedded layers beneath. Outline line work, hatching on cut material. Everything here is drawn many times its true size. No word, digit or label appears, and no border. The points are well spread.

**Geometry to be drawn**

One upright hatched column hangs from a fragment of hatched slab at the top of the sheet, with white paper at its left and right. That fragment carries no numeral. The column keeps one width, bounded by one vertical line at each side. One horizontal line crosses it and divides it into an upper part and a lower part, both drawn deep enough to take a point well inside the hatching, with no second horizontal line anywhere on the column.

An open white gap, drawn tall, runs across the sheet below the foot of the column. Below that gap lie three hatched bands, one above another, each spanning the full width, separated by one horizontal line, and each drawn deep.

- The perimeter member 24 is the upper part of the column. Identified at the centre of that upper part, midway between its side lines and well above the dividing line.
- The low-friction facing 28 is the lower part of the column, between the dividing line and the foot of the column. Identified at the centre of that lower part, midway between the dividing line above and the foot line below and midway between the side lines, so the point lies on neither line and in neither the upper part nor the gap.
- The bearing face 26 is the horizontal line at the foot of the column, where the column ends and the gap begins. Identified at the mid-point of that foot line, and not on either side line.
- The clearance 34 is the gap between the foot of the column and the top of the first band, drawn tall enough that column and band nowhere touch. Identified within that gap directly below the middle of the column, midway between the foot line and the top edge of the first band.
- The covering element 36 is the first, uppermost band. Identified at its mid-depth toward its right end, clear of the gap above it and of the line below it.
- The exposed face 38 is the top edge of that first band, where the gap meets the hatching. Identified at one point on that line in the left quarter of the sheet, well clear of the column, and not on the line between the first and second bands.
- The bonding material 40 is the second band. Identified at its mid-depth toward its left end, clear of the lines above and below it.
- The substrate 42 is the third band, its lower edge drawn above the bottom of the sheet. Identified at its mid-depth toward its right end, clear of the line above it and of its lower edge.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 24, 26, 28, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment, device drawn by a flexible pulli

**View:** Three-quarter perspective from above, as FIG. 1 but from a greater distance, so that several laid tiles are in frame. Outline line work. The sheet contains only the parts listed. No word, letter, digit or label appears, no border, bar, band or filled area, and nothing is drawn below the floor.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The floor fills the sheet: a few large square tiles in perspective, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours, and otherwise plain. The device stands on a tile at the middle right of the floor. One ring stands at the near left end of its slab, and no other ring, loop or hook appears anywhere on the sheet.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole assembly standing on that tile, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing toward its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. The assembly is drawn large and the slab has clearly visible thickness, so its near front side face is a long band of plain paper tall enough to take a point well inside it. Identified within that face, in its half nearer the right end of the slab and midway up its height, so the point lies at the end remote from the ring, and not on the ring, the cord, either housing, the column, the floor or a joint line.
- The attachment formation 48 is that ring at the near left end of the slab, low on that end and touching it: a single loop of one continuous outline enclosing one opening, like a plain washer seen at an angle. It is not interlinked rings, a chain or a knot. It is drawn large and stands clear of the slab end, so its opening is plainly visible. Identified at the topmost point of the ring's outline, and not on the slab, the cord or the floor.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is a slack cord running from that ring away to the left, sagging gently and passing off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep, without doubling back or looping. It is slender and of even width, with no core line, and no block, plug, connector, knot, ring or arrowhead appears at its end or along it. Identified on the cord midway between the ring and the left edge of the sheet, and not on the ring, the slab or the floor.
- The covering element 36 is one of the tiles of that floor. The tile in the lower left of the sheet is drawn large, with no cord crossing it and no joint line within it. Identified at the centre of that tile, well inside its edges and clear of the device, the cord and the ring.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 36, 46, 48

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10
- 36
- 46
- 48

**View:** Greatly enlarged fragmentary vertical section through the lower end of a perimeter member of the kind shown in FIG. 2, at a place where the clearance is present, with the bedded layers beneath. Hatching on cut material. Everything here is drawn many times its true size. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

One upright hatched column hangs from a fragment of hatched slab at the top of the sheet, with white paper at its left and right. That fragment carries no numeral. The column keeps one width, bounded by one vertical line at each side. One horizontal line crosses it and divides it into an upper part and a lower part, both drawn deep enough to take a point well inside the hatching, with no second horizontal line anywhere on the column.

An open white gap, drawn tall, runs across the sheet below the foot of the column. Below that gap lie three hatched bands, one above another, each spanning the full width, separated by one horizontal line, and each drawn deep.

- The perimeter member 24 is the upper part of the column. Identified at the centre of that upper part, midway between its side lines and well above the dividing line.
- The low-friction facing 28 is the lower part of the column, between the dividing line and the foot of the column. Identified at the centre of that lower part, midway between the dividing line above and the foot line below and midway between the side lines, clear of all four lines.
- The bearing face 26 is the horizontal line at the foot of the column, where column ends and gap begins. Identified at the mid-point of that foot line, and not on either side line.
- The clearance 34 is the gap between the foot of the column and the top of the first band, drawn tall enough that column and band nowhere touch. Identified within that gap directly below the middle of the column, midway between the foot line above and the band below.
- The covering element 36 is the first, uppermost band. Identified at its mid-depth toward its right end, clear of the gap above and the line below.
- The exposed face 38 is the top edge of that first band, where the gap meets the hatching. Identified at one point on that line in the left quarter of the sheet, well clear of the column, and not on the line below it.
- The bonding material 40 is the second band. Identified at its mid-depth toward its left end, clear of the lines above and below.
- The substrate 42 is the third band, its lower edge above the bottom of the sheet. Identified at its mid-depth toward its right end, clear of the line above and its lower edge.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 24, 26, 28, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42

content.text:
I repaired the two leader-placement failures at their geometric root and left the invention untouched.

**FIG. 4, numeral 28 in a rejected coordinate cluster.** The old brief forced the low-friction facing into a "short lower part" of the column and additionally required the clearance gap to be drawn taller than it, so the only region available to 28 was a sliver squeezed between the dividing line above and the bearing-face line at the foot, with 24, 26 and 34 all crowding it. The brief now divides the column into an upper part and a lower part that are both drawn deep enough to take a point well inside the hatching, drops the constraint that tied the gap height to the facing height, and gives 28 a single constructed point: the centre of the lower part, midway between the dividing line above and the foot line below and midway between the side lines, clear of all four lines. This does not change the invention. The specification still says the low-friction facing 28 is thin and hard, and FIG. 4 is already described in the text as an enlarged detail drawn many times true size, which the brief now states in the view line.

**FIG. 5, numeral 10 landing on the ring and losing its terminal dot.** The old target put 10 on the near left side face of the slab, which is the same end of the slab the attachment formation 48 projects from, so the two targets were neighbours and the endpoint drifted onto the ring. The device is now identified on the near front side face of the slab, in the half nearer the right end, explicitly at the end remote from the ring, with the exclusion list retained. The ring stays where the description puts it, low on the near left end.

**FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3.** These three failed at image generation with a provider 429, not on their content. I left FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 as they were so that previously clean geometry is not disturbed, and removed one invented proportion from FIG. 1 (the pump housing described as the largest body, taller and wider than the motor block), which the specification does not state. The sheets need regeneration from these briefs.

**Length.** Checking the briefs against the 2800-character limit found FIG. 4 at 3237 and FIG. 5 at 2950 after the repairs. Both were shortened by removing invented rendering constraints and redundant phrasing rather than required relationships; all five files are now 2316 to 2790 characters.

Numeral-to-sheet assignments (8/8/3/8/4), the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the Detailed Description, and the claims are unchanged and remain in step.

input.summary: Repaired all five sheets listed in the review. FIG. 4: numeral 28 had no room, because the brief made the low-friction facing a short sliver and then required the clearance gap to be taller than it, so the only available region sat between the dividing line and the foot line with three other targets crowding it; the column is now divided into an upper and a lower part both drawn deep enough to hold a point, the gap-height constraint tied to the facing was dropped, and 28 has one constructed target at the centre of the lower part, clear of all four bounding lines. FIG. 5: numeral 10 pointed at the near left side face of the slab, the same end the ring projects from, so the endpoint drifted onto the ring and lost its terminal dot; 10 now points into the near front side face in the half nearer the right end, explicitly at the end remote from the ring. FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 failed at image generation with a provider 429 rather than on content, so FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 were left intact and FIG. 1 only lost one invented proportion (the pump housing called the largest body). Length checking then showed the two repaired briefs over the 2800-character limit, so both were tightened by removing invented rendering constraints and redundancy; all five files are now between 2316 and 2790 characters. No claim, description, numeral definition, embodiment, or numeral-to-sheet assignment was changed.
reasoning: The FIG. 4 failure was a geometry-authoring fault, not a rendering accident. The brief itself made numeral 28 unplaceable: it called the facing the 'short lower part', then separately required the clearance to be 'drawn taller than the short lower part', which locks the facing into a sliver whose interior is within a few pixels of the dividing line above, the foot line below, and the endpoints for 24, 26 and 34. Any endpoint the renderer chose there was going to sit in a cluster the reviewers reject. Removing the coupling between gap height and facing height, and letting both parts of the column be drawn deep, gives the point somewhere to exist.

I resisted the tempting shortcut of deleting numeral 28 from FIG. 4 or moving it to another sheet. The low-friction facing is the member that actually touches the tile in the FIG. 4 embodiment and is what claim 4 recites, so it has to be labelled somewhere, and FIG. 4 is the only sectional view enlarged enough to show it as distinct from the perimeter member that carries it.

Drawing the facing deep on FIG. 4 does not contradict the specification statement that the facing is thin and hard. FIG. 4 is described in the text as an enlarged fragmentary detail in which the clearance is drawn many times its true height, so an enlarged proportion on that sheet is already the disclosed convention; I moved that convention into the view line of the brief rather than adding anything to the specification.

The FIG. 5 failure had an obvious spatial cause that the negative exclusion list could not fix by itself. Telling the renderer 'not on the ring' while pointing it at the slab face immediately adjacent to the ring is asking it to thread a needle. The fix was to separate the two targets along the length of the slab, putting the device numeral at the opposite end from the attachment formation, and to keep the exclusion list as a second line of defence. The missing terminal dot should follow, since it was a downstream symptom of the rejected placement.

For FIG. 1 through FIG. 3 the correct action was mostly restraint. Those three sheets never got drawn, so nothing is known to be wrong with their geometry, and rewriting briefs that previously cleared geometry and leader review would risk trading a transient capacity error for a real defect. The single change I made to FIG. 1 removes a constraint the specification does not support: nothing in the disclosure says the air-extraction mechanism is the largest body or that it is taller and wider than the motor.

Trimming to the 2800-character limit was done by cutting invented rendering constraints and duplicated wording, never a relationship the text requires. What survived in every case is the identity of each numbered part, its position relative to the others, and one unambiguous endpoint per numeral.
changes: figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-FRAGMENTARY-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBE.md: the column is now divided by one horizontal line into an upper part (24) and a lower part (28), both drawn deep enough to take a point well inside the hatching; the constraint making the clearance taller than the facing was removed and replaced by a gap drawn tall enough that column and band nowhere touch; numeral 28 now has a constructed target at the centre of the lower part, midway between the dividing line and the foot line and midway between the side lines, clear of all four lines; numeral 34 now targets the gap directly below the middle of the column, midway between the foot line and the band; the brief was shortened from 3237 to 2790 characters.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-DEVICE-DRAWN-BY-A-FLEXIBLE-PULLI.md: numeral 10 moved from the near left side face of the slab, adjacent to the ring, to the near front side face in the half nearer the right end, stated as the end remote from the ring, with the exclusion list retained; the floor and the single-ring condition are now stated once in an opening paragraph; the brief was shortened from 2950 to 2744 characters. Numerals 10, 36, 46 and 48 all remain on this sheet.

figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: removed the unsupported proportion describing the air-extraction mechanism as the largest body, taller and wider than the motor block.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn, since no claim, description, or Background text was touched. Claim 1 still turns on the rigid, deliberately non-sealing perimeter member with a low-friction bearing face, a clearance through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric pressure against that continuous inflow, an all-rigid path from motor to tile, and sliding while the pressure differential is maintained. That combination clears DE-202021002652-U1, which vibrates shafts ending in rubber-elastic suction cups; US-11408462-B2, whose wall-contacting member is an elastic partition merely restrained by a stiffer frame; US-4934475-A, which recites a seal member and uses vibration to reduce the suction-adhering force so the body walks along the wall; US-11247858-B2, a perforated suction plate for lifting sheet goods; and US-10001245-B2, whose pneumatic generator holds in suction mode and floats the plate on an air cushion in blower mode as mutually exclusive states. The drawing repairs were checked against this: FIG. 4 still shows the clearance and the rigid facing that are the distinguishing features, and FIG. 5 still shows the flexible pulling element and the low attachment formation that carry independent claim 15.
